title: Automatic singing assessment & practice feedback

findings.title: Evaluation Framework for Automatic Singing Transcription
findings.finding: Defines the note-level tolerances the MIR field actually uses, taken from MIREX: a transcribed note has a CORRECT ONSET if it lands within +/-50 ms of the ground-truth onset; CORRECT PITCH if within +/-0.5 semitone (+/-50 cents); CORRECT OFFSET if within max(50 ms, 20% of the ground-truth note duration). Correctness is reported at three strictness levels (COnPOff = onset+pitch+offset, COnP = onset+pitch, COn = onset only) plus named error classes: Only-Bad-Onset, Only-Bad-Pitch, Only-Bad-Offset, Split (one sung note transcribed as several), Merge, spurious, missing. Crucially, the two expert annotators (10 and 7 years of music training, annotating to agreement) were instructed that ornaments -- pitch bending at note starts and VIBRATO -- are NOT separate notes, and that PORTAMENTO between two notes does not create a third note; onsets are placed at the start of the voiced vowel, not the consonant. Corpus: 38 melodies, 1154 s total, all UNTRAINED singers -- 14 children's songs (557 s) from 8 children aged 5-11, 13 pop melodies (315 s) from 8 adult male untrained singers, 11 pop melodies (281 s) from 5 adult female untrained singers (adults from MTG-QBH). Per-note ground-truth pitch is annotated at cents resolution with an explicit per-note tuning deviation.
findings.implication: Adopt these exact windows as the companion's default scoring contract (+/-50 ms onset, +/-50 cents pitch, offset max(50 ms, 20%)), and copy the annotation rule as a SEGMENTATION rule: vibrato and portamento must be absorbed into the note they decorate before any cents error is computed, or a good singer's ornament is scored as a split note plus a pitch error.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Singing Voice Accuracy: A Comparison Between Subjective and Objective Methods
findings.finding: 166 UNTRAINED adult singers (57 men, 109 women) each sang 'Happy Birthday' a cappella; 18 experts (speech therapists specialising in voice, and musicians) rated global pitch accuracy of all 166 takes. Inter-judge agreement: median Spearman r = 0.77 (SD 0.08, p<0.01); downsampling to random subgroups showed THREE judges already give a panel mean correlating above 0.85, so large juries buy little. Mean absolute pitch-interval deviation in cents correlated with the expert panel mean at Spearman r = -0.87 (p<0.01). A three-predictor regression (interval deviation, number of tonality modulations, number of melodic contour errors) explained 81% of the variance in judges' scores (F = 232.17, p<0.001), but only two predictors carried it: interval deviation (beta = .51, t = -6.61, p<0.001) and tonality modulations (beta = -.45, t = -6.33, p<0.001). Melodic contour errors did NOT contribute (beta = .08, t = 1.89, p = .06) -- a null result the authors attribute to their rarity. A 'tonality modulation' is operationally defined as an interval error larger than 100 cents that is NOT followed by a corrective interval of at least 100 cents in the reverse direction. The interval-deviation-to-rating relationship is LOGARITHMIC: judges discriminated finely among accurate singers but barely distinguished slightly inaccurate from very inaccurate performances.
findings.implication: Score a take as mean absolute interval deviation in cents PLUS a count of uncorrected key drifts, and compress the display logarithmically -- a linear cents-to-score mapping over-punishes the struggling singer in exactly the range where real listeners stop discriminating, and under-resolves the range where they do.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Singing Voice Accuracy (self-evaluation sub-analysis)
findings.finding: In the same 166 untrained adult singers, each singer rated their own accuracy immediately after singing. Self-evaluation correlated only r = -0.35 (p<0.01) with the objective interval-deviation measure and r = 0.35 (p<0.01) with the 18-judge panel mean -- i.e. singers account for roughly 12% of the variance in how accurate they actually were. The miscalibration runs in BOTH directions and is asymmetric by skill: 41% of the inaccurate singers (panel score < 4, N = 39) OVERestimated themselves (self-rating > 4), while 63% of the very accurate singers (panel score > 6, N = 84) UNDERvalued themselves (self-rating < 6).
findings.implication: The companion's number will contradict the student's self-image most of the time, and in opposite directions for the two groups it serves: expect to have to justify a low score to a confident weak singer and a high score to a self-doubting strong one, so pair every score with located evidence (which note, how many cents) rather than shipping a bare number.

findings.title: Pitch Perception in Music: Do Scoops Matter?
findings.finding: Across three experiments, 110 participants judged which of two four-tone melodies was more in tune, in a pairwise-comparison paradigm. Stimulus design was calibrated to REAL singing (scoop statistics measured from the Pfordresher & Mantell 2014 corpus): scoops -- the brief pitch transition into or out of a target note -- were synthesised into the initial or final 220 ms of a tone, just under 25% of its total duration, with magnitudes taken from human singers, e.g. 74 cents for an upward starting scoop that preserves melodic continuity versus 58 cents for a downward one; the steady-state 'asymptote' was set in tune or mistuned by +/-50 cents (a quarter tone). Result: intonation judgements were significantly shifted by the scoops alone, F(3,49) = 39.694, p<.001, partial eta-squared = .71, revealing two coexisting mechanisms -- partial statistical averaging of pitch across the whole tone (so a scoop that compensates a mistuned asymptote is PREFERRED) and evaluation of the scoop relative to surrounding melodic context. The authors note scoops are deterministic and goal-directed, not motor noise.
findings.implication: Frame-level cents error is the wrong metric for the first and last ~220 ms of every sung note: real singers routinely deviate 58-74 cents there, listeners integrate rather than penalise it, so score the steady-state portion (or a duration-weighted mean) and treat the transition window separately, or the companion reports a large error where a teacher hears none.

findings.title: The mistuning perception test: A new measurement instrument
findings.finding: Calibration sample N = 333 listeners (227 women, 106 men), aged 18-70 (M = 24.76, SD = 7.95), 185 tested in the lab and 148 online, Gold-MSI musical-training raw scores spanning 7 to 48 (M = 24.21, SD = 10.94). Task: 2-alternative forced choice on 6-12 s excerpts of REAL pop performances (MedleyDB) in which the vocal track was pitch-shifted 10-100 cents in 5-cent steps, sharp and flat, against the unaltered instrumental backing. Measured thresholds: 95% of participant abilities fell in a pitch-shift range of 36.3 to 82.6 cents, with a MEDIAN of 55.0 cents. Musical training moves the threshold but does not abolish it: a low Gold-MSI training raw score of 10 corresponds to a 65.2-cent mistuning-perception threshold, a high raw score of 40 to a 43.2-cent threshold. Test-retest reliability r = .698 (95% CI [.544, .806]) with 30 items, falling to r = .579 with 15. Validation sample N = 66.
findings.implication: The +/-50-cent convention is not arbitrary -- it sits at the median human detection threshold for mistuning in real, accompanied singing -- so flagging errors far below ~40 cents reports deviations the student's own audience cannot hear; the flag threshold should arguably widen for beginners (own threshold ~65 cents) and narrow for trained users.

findings.title: The Evaluation of Vocal Pitch Accuracy: The Case of Operatic Singing Voices
findings.finding: 22 professional musicians (8 women, 14 men, aged 26-73) ranked 14 operatic excerpts sung by 14 different professional or semi-professional singers, using pairwise comparison in a test and a retest. Two judges (numbers 2 and 12) exceeded the chi-squared intra-judge instability threshold (12.592 at 6 df) and were excluded; the remaining 20 showed strong inter-judge reliability (no singer's rank variance exceeded the 14.067 threshold). The method point that matters for scoring: because vibrato was present (mainly on final tones), mean F0 for each note was computed over COMPLETE VIBRATO CYCLES only, and interval size in cents derived from those means -- e.g. a nominal 200-cent interval produced as 150 or 250 cents counts as a 50-cent deviation. A multiple regression on six objective parameters (pitch interval deviation, average tempo, F0 of the starting note, energy distribution, vibrato rate, vibrato extent) explained 78.8% of the variance in judges' ratings (all-interactions model 82.7%), and several significant interaction terms were JUDGE-SPECIFIC: for some judges vibrato rate and extent materially shifted their pitch-accuracy verdict, for others they did not.
findings.implication: For any note carrying vibrato, average F0 over whole vibrato cycles before computing cents error -- and accept that a single scalar 'pitch accuracy' number cannot reproduce expert opinion on a trained voice, because the experts themselves differ in how much vibrato quality feeds their pitch verdict.

findings.title: An automatic singing skill evaluation method for unknown melodies using pitch interval accuracy and vibrato features
findings.finding: Reference-free (no score, no target melody) good/poor classification from two feature families. Pitch interval accuracy: the F0 trajectory is low-pass filtered at 5 Hz, silent sections removed, then matched against a Gaussian comb filter on the 100-cent semitone grid with standard deviation sigma = 16 cents; the sharpness of the resulting long-term offset distribution measures how well the singer sits on ANY semitone grid, independent of key. Vibrato: detected with rate constrained to 5-8 Hz and extent to 30-150 cents, with F0 transitions wider than a 300-cent threshold excluded as note changes rather than vibrato. Data: 600 samples from 12 singers drawn from the 100-subject AIST Humming Database, each singing 50 excerpts of 25 Japanese or English RWC songs after hearing each excerpt five times; the 12 singers were selected as consistently 'good' or consistently 'poor' in a prior human rank-ordering study (Nakano, Goto & Hiraga, ICMPC 2006). Leave-one-out on the combined male-female set: 83.5% average classification rate (precision_good 87.6%, recall_good 78.0%, precision_poor 70.3%, recall_poor 89.0%). Named failure modes: a good singer with NO vibrato is misclassified as poor, and a poor singer with unstable F0 is misread as producing vibrato.
findings.implication: Gives concrete detector bands for the vibrato gate a practice companion needs (5-8 Hz rate, 30-150 cents extent, >300 cents = a real note change, sigma 16 cents around the grid) -- and warns that presence-of-vibrato must never earn scoring credit, because absence of vibrato in a competent singer and instability in an incompetent one are the two errors this feature family makes.

findings.title: A technical framework for automatic perceptual evaluation of singing quality (PESnQ)
findings.finding: 20 recordings, each by a DIFFERENT singer -- 10 singing ABBA's 'I Have A Dream' (2 min), 10 singing 'Edelweiss' -- spanning amateur to professional, split into 120 short utterances. 5 professional-musician judges (Western classical, contemporary, and Chinese-orchestra backgrounds) rated overall quality plus 7 named perceptual parameters (intonation, rhythm consistency, appropriate vibrato, voice quality/timbre, articulation, relative volume, pitch dynamic range) on a 1-5 Likert scale. Human ceiling: average inter-judge Pearson correlation on the overall-quality question was 0.82, with all parameter questions above 0.60. A linear combination of the judges' OWN parameter scores predicted their own overall score at Pearson 0.966 in 10-fold CV -- humans really do compose an overall verdict from parameters -- and intonation correlated 0.910 with the vibrato rating. Machine performance depended sharply on granularity: the best acoustic feature set reached only Pearson 0.59 against human ratings at UTTERANCE level, but 0.904 at SONG level via late fusion (0.725 via early fusion), both p<0.001.
findings.implication: A whole-take score can approach the human inter-judge ceiling, but per-phrase scores from the same features land near 0.59 -- so present phrase-level output as located EVIDENCE (this note, this many cents, this late) and reserve graded quality judgements for the whole take.

findings.title: Assessment of Student Music Performances Using Deep Neural Networks
findings.finding: Florida Bandmasters Association all-state audition recordings, 2013-2015, alto saxophone / Bb clarinet / flute (INSTRUMENTAL wind playing, not sung -- read the transfer to singing with that caveat): 1410 Middle School (grades 7-8) and 1550 Symphonic Band (grades 11-12) technical-exercise performances, expert-graded on Musicality, Note Accuracy, Rhythmic Accuracy and Tone Quality. Best model Pearson correlations with expert ratings: Symphonic Band M 0.744 / N 0.694 / R 0.743 / T 0.649; Middle School M 0.724 / N 0.666 / R 0.630 / T 0.634 (all significant at p<=0.05), beating a hand-crafted-feature SVR baseline (e.g. Symphonic Musicality 0.612). The decisive negative result is cross-proficiency transfer: a Musicality model trained on Middle School and tested on Symphonic Band reached only R2 = 0.193, and the reverse direction R2 = -0.106; for Note Accuracy and Rhythmic Accuracy the cross-category average was R2 = -0.765 -- far WORSE than simply predicting the mean. The paper also states plainly that for this dataset 'the number of judges and the grading rubrics are not available'.
findings.implication: Do not ship one assessment model across skill levels: an accuracy scorer fitted on beginners actively mispredicts advanced performers and vice versa, so the companion needs proficiency-conditioned scoring or per-user calibration -- and discount any published correlation whose ground-truth rater count and rubric are undocumented.

findings.title: Perception of just noticeable time displacement of a tone presented in a metrical sequence at different tempos
findings.id: STL-QPSR (KTH Speech, Music and Hearing) 33(4):97-108; no DOI
findings.finding: 30 listeners of varied musical background (almost all amateurs; one professional musician) adjusted the timing of the FOURTH tone in a six-tone metrical sequence until they heard the sequence as perfectly regular, at constant inter-onset intervals varied from 100 ms to 1000 ms. The average just-noticeable time displacement was about 10 ms for tones shorter than about 240 ms, and about 5% of the duration for longer tones. Subjects' musical training did not appear to affect these values. (The companion study Friberg & Sundberg 1995, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 98(5):2524-2531, DOI:10.1121/1.413218, is widely cited for a smaller 6 ms / 2.5% figure under a different discrimination paradigm; that paper was NOT read primary in this wave and its numbers are not asserted here.)
findings.implication: Sets the honest floor for rhythm feedback: at a 600 ms beat (100 bpm) a listener needs roughly 30 ms of displacement to hear lateness at all, so the standard +/-50 ms MIR onset window is already MORE forgiving than a human ear at moderate tempo and much more forgiving at fast tempo -- a fixed 50 ms window under-reports rushing in slow ballads and over-reports it in fast passages; scale as max(10 ms, 5% of the notated duration).

findings.title: The effect of visual and auditory feedback on adult poor-pitch remediation
findings.finding: Randomised pretest-posttest control-group design. N = 84 recruited (University at Buffalo n=56, Northwestern n=28), 75 retained after inclusion criteria (which required a pitch-discrimination threshold below 100 cents); adults, M age 21.75 (SD 8.02, range 18-70), 84% with no instrumental training and 94% with no singing training. Random assignment to 20 minutes of: visual feedback with auditory doubling (n=25; an iPad app drawing the singer's f0 line against the target), auditory-only feedback (n=23), or an active control imitating foreign-language speech (n=27). Outcome measure: the Seattle Singing Accuracy Protocol, with a sung note counted as an error when it deviated more than 50 CENTS from target. All three groups improved from pre to post. Only the visual group's percent improvement differed from zero, t(24) = 2.55, p = .009; visual vs control was significant, t(46) = 1.8, p = .039, d = 0.49; auditory vs control was NOT, p = .14, d = 0.29. Critically, the one-factor ANOVA across all three conditions was NOT significant and indicated a small effect size. Restricting to participants making at least 20% errors at pretest: visual vs control t(37) = 1.75, p = .044, d = 0.54; auditory improved from zero (p = .041) but still not above control (p = .170, d = 0.36).
findings.implication: Twenty minutes of a real-time pitch line buys about half a standard deviation for adults who start out inaccurate, and nothing detectable for those who do not -- so gate the visual display on measured pretest error rather than showing it to everyone, and do not over-claim: the omnibus test in the best-controlled study of this question was null.

findings.title: The effect of concurrent visual feedback on adult singing accuracy
findings.finding: NULL RESULT over a realistic training horizon. University students NOT majoring in music (adult non-musicians) were randomly assigned to two groups and played the computer game SingingCoach for 10 weeks; the treatment group received concurrent visual feedback on singing accuracy, the control group received none. Both groups improved their pitch-accuracy scores significantly over the 10 weeks, but the treatment group did NOT score significantly higher than the control group. Participants' ratings of their own singing rose significantly in both groups. The authors' own conclusion is that singing MORE OFTEN is what helped, with concurrent feedback adding no detectable increment. CAVEAT ON N: the group sizes are not stated in the publicly accessible abstract and the full text is paywalled, so the participant count could not be verified in this wave. Zhang 2026 (DOI:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920074) characterises this literature as showing that a group given 10 weeks of concurrent visual feedback performed better during training but converged with controls on a retention test after feedback removal -- classic guidance dependency.
findings.implication: Over 10 weeks the dose that mattered was time-on-task, not the pitch display -- so make sessions-completed the companion's primary success metric, and make any continuous on-screen pitch line fadeable or withdrawn on retention trials, because a feature that only improves performance while it is visible has not taught anything.

findings.title: Acoustic spectral feedback in vocal learning: a systematic review of psychological mechanisms and skill outcomes
findings.finding: Systematic review (OSF-registered, osf.io/qgwxk; CC BY 4.0) of 36 peer-reviewed studies, approximately 2,850 participants in total, individual study N ranging from 1 to 334 with a MEDIAN of only 48; populations span singing learners, music-major vocal students, and beginner-to-professional singers, plus 14 instrumental studies included where the psychological mechanism transfers. The review reports NO pooled effect sizes -- heterogeneity forced narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis, which is itself the honest state of this evidence base. Two findings a builder must carry: (a) an explicit cognitive-load versus guidance-dependency trade-off, in which real-time spectral displays impose extraneous cognitive load because learners must process both the phonatory action and the constantly changing visual information on screen, with beginners most at risk of overload; (b) a null transfer result -- although one included study's experimental group scored significantly higher on metacognition, F(1,78) = 5.10, p = 0.03, partial eta-squared = 0.06, that metacognitive improvement did NOT significantly predict improvement in singing performance, t = 0.23, p = 0.82. One instrumental study reported performance self-efficacy at d = 0.58.
findings.implication: Design the display for the load budget rather than for information density: show one thing at a time during phonation and move everything else to post-take review -- and do not treat a student who has become better at TALKING about their pitch as one who has become better at singing it, because that transfer measures at essentially zero.

findings.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes over 23,663 observations (domain-general across task types, NOT music-specific -- treat as a design prior, not a singing result): feedback interventions improved performance on average by d = .41, BUT over one third of feedback interventions DECREASED performance, and this could not be explained by sampling error, by feedback sign (praise vs criticism), or by existing theories. The proposed Feedback Intervention Theory attributes it to locus of attention across three hierarchically ordered levels -- task learning, task motivation, and meta-task/self processes -- with the empirical moderator result that feedback effectiveness DECREASES as attention moves up the hierarchy toward the self and away from the task.
findings.implication: The single most load-bearing design rule for a practice companion: keep every message pointed at the task ('bar 12 beat 3 sat 40 cents flat and entered 90 ms late') and never at the person ('your intonation is weak', skill grades, leaderboards), because self-directed feedback is the mechanism by which more than a third of feedback interventions make performance worse.

gaps: Could not find any automatic SINGING assessment system validated against expert human raters on a sample of TRAINED singers larger than a few dozen: the biggest expert-validated singing sets located were 166 untrained singers with 18 judges (Larrouy-Maestri 2013) and 20 singers with 5 judges (Gupta 2018), while everything at thousands of performances (FBA, 2960 recordings) is instrumental wind playing, and the one large singing set (MAST, 1018 performances) carries only unanimous binary pass/fail labels and a non-commercial licence. Found no study at all that isolates the effect of RHYTHM or timing feedback on singing -- every intervention study located manipulated pitch feedback only -- so the millisecond tolerances in finding 10 come from psychoacoustic discrimination experiments on tone sequences (N=30 listeners) and have never, as far as this search reached, been validated as a pedagogically useful threshold for a singer; nor could any source be found stating what timing tolerance an expert singing teacher actually applies in a lesson. No pooled effect size exists for visual feedback in vocal learning: the 2026 systematic review of 36 studies explicitly declined to meta-analyse because of heterogeneity (median study N = 48), and the retention / guidance-dependency picture rests on a handful of paywalled studies. Finally, no source was found giving a measured cents or millisecond threshold at which a practice tool's feedback becomes DISCOURAGING -- the strongest evidence on that question (Kluger & DeNisi) is domain-general and thirty years old -- and two secondary summaries encountered during this wave DISAGREED about whether Wilson, Lee, Callaghan & Thorpe (2008, Journal of Interdisciplinary Music Studies 2(1&2):157-172) found that real-time visual feedback HARMED skilled singers through added cognitive load; the primary could not be retrieved, so that claim is deliberately excluded from the findings above rather than repeated.
